generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this means a module's outcomes are worth reading before you do anything else with it. Each one uses a verb that signals the kind of performance expected, whether that is to describe, to apply, to analyse or to evaluate, and that verb is a strong clue to how the assessment will be marked. Checking your work against the outcomes as you go is a quick way to see whether you are doing what the module actually asks.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students read the same learning outcome from their module handbook: Evaluate the usefulness of a common method in your field.

Student A reads it quickly and starts describing the method: what it is, how it works, where it is used. The writing is accurate, but it only describes. The outcome asked for something the writing never does.

Student B reads the same outcome and breaks it down first. The verb is evaluate, which means weighing strengths against weaknesses to reach a judgement. What it is about is the method's usefulness, not simply how it works. And demonstrating it means coming to a reasoned view, backed by evidence, about when the method helps and when it does not. Student B then writes to exactly that.

Both students know the method. Only Student B answered the outcome, because only Student B worked out what it was actually asking.
generatedProse.summary: Learning outcomes are the statements of what each module expects you to be able to do, and they are where your assessment points. You can now find the outcomes in your own module's documentation, and break one down into its active verb and what it asks you to demonstrate. Reading outcomes this way turns a vague aim into a clear target, and it is a habit that will help in every module you take.

check.body: You are breaking down a learning outcome from your own subject that begins with the verb 'analyse'. Which of these shows you have understood what that verb asks for?

items.text: Separating something into its parts, examining how they relate, and saying what that shows.
Listing everything you can remember about the topic.
Giving your personal opinion of the topic.
Describing the topic clearly from start to finish.

feedback.correct: That's right. 'Analyse' asks you to break something into its parts, examine how they relate, and show what that reveals, not to list, describe or simply give an opinion.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what 'analyse' does that listing, describing or giving an opinion does not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: 'Analyse' asks you to separate something into its parts, examine how they relate, and draw out what that shows. Listing is recall, describing is just an account, and an opinion alone has no working behind it.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
